text:
The usual way is called byte pair encoding, or BPE, and you can run it by hand. Here's a tiny training text. Low, five times. Lower, twice. Newest, three times. And widest, twice. Split every word into characters, with a marker for where the word ends. Now count every pair of neighbours. L and O sit side by side seven times, and so do O and W. Merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol, write the merge down, and count again. L and O first. Then that with W, making low. Then low at the end of a word. Then E and S, then T, then the word end. Nobody told it about suffixes. Est ends both newest and widest, so it earned its merges early. After ten merges, low and newest are single tokens. Widest is still four pieces, because wid never came up often enough. And that list of merges is the tokenizer. New text gets split into characters, and the merges are replayed in order. Frequent text ends up as cheap, whole tokens. Rare text stays in pieces. And the pieces are what you pay for.

Underneath every token there are bytes. An English letter is one byte. A Japanese or Hindi character is three. This tokenizer starts from bytes, and merges what it saw often. Hello in Japanese is fifteen bytes, and just one token. In Hindi, eighteen bytes make four. But in Tifinagh, a Berber script it rarely saw, hello is twelve bytes... and twelve tokens.
